items.topic: sampling-t2 · unbiasedness and variance of stratified and simple-random-sampling means
items.stem: A population of size N is divided into L strata of sizes N₁,…,N_L. A stratified random sample of size n is drawn, with n_j units selected by simple random sampling within stratum j. Let ȳ_j be the sample mean in stratum j and define ȳ_st=∑_{j=1}^L(N_j/N)ȳ_j. An independent simple random sample of size n is also drawn from the population, with sample mean ȳ and variance of the sample mean σ². Which statements are correct?
statements: ȳ_st is an unbiased estimator of the population mean.
ȳ is an unbiased estimator of the population mean.
The variance σ²_st of ȳ_st is always less than or equal to σ².
If n_j/N_j=n/N for every stratum j, then σ²_st=σ².

A.why: Each stratum sample mean is design-unbiased for its stratum population mean, so their population-weighted sum is unbiased. The ordinary SRS sample mean is also unbiased.

B.why: Under simple random sampling, the sample mean is design-unbiased for the population mean.

C.why: Proportional allocation does not generally make the two variances equal. The stratified variance depends on within-stratum variation, while SRS variance also reflects between-stratum variation.

D.why: Statements 3 and 4 are not universal identities; proportional allocation alone does not imply equal variances.

items.explanation: For each stratum j, simple random sampling within that stratum gives E(ȳ_j)=Ȳ_j, the stratum population mean. Therefore E(ȳ_st)=∑(N_j/N)Ȳ_j=Ȳ, so statement 1 is true. An ordinary simple random sample mean is also unbiased for the population mean, so statement 2 is true. The variance of a stratified estimator is not always smaller than the SRS variance: the allocation across strata matters, and an inefficient allocation can increase variance. Thus statement 3 is false as a universal claim. Under proportional allocation, n_j/N_j=n/N, the variance expression still involves the within-stratum variances. The SRS variance involves the overall population variance, which includes both within- and between-stratum components. They are not generally equal, so statement 4 is false. Hence only statements 1 and 2 are correct. Other-exam relevance: stratified sampling, unbiasedness and design variance are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi; This is topic overlap, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those other examinations.

items.topic: sampling-t10 · simple random sampling with and without replacement; unbiasedness and finite-population correction
items.stem: A sample of size n is drawn from a finite population of N households, where 0<n<N, to estimate the proportion of households with more than one earning member. Sample I is selected by simple random sampling without replacement, and Sample II by simple random sampling with replacement. Let p₁ and p₂ be the respective sample proportions, and let σᵢ²=Var(pᵢ), i=1,2. Which statements are true?
statements: p₁ is unbiased for the population proportion, but p₂ is not.
p₂ is unbiased for the population proportion, but p₁ is not.

A.why: Both sample proportions are unbiased for the population proportion under their respective simple random sampling designs.

B.why: Sampling with replacement does not introduce bias in the sample proportion; both estimators are unbiased.

C.why: For 0<n<N, sampling without replacement has the finite-population correction (N−n)/(N−1), reducing the variance relative to sampling with replacement.

D.why: The variance ordering is the reverse: without-replacement sampling has lower variance for the sample proportion.

items.explanation: Let P be the fixed population proportion. Under either design, each draw or selected unit has expectation P, so both sample proportions are unbiased; statements 1 and 2 are false. Under SRSWR, the draws are independent Bernoulli(P), giving Var(p₂)=P(1−P)/n. Under SRSWOR, Var(p₁)=P(1−P)/n × (N−n)/(N−1). For 1<n<N, this finite-population correction is strictly below one, so statement 3 is true. Important boundary note: when n=1, the correction equals one and the two variances are equal. The printed question states only 0<n<N, so its strict inequality omits this n=1 exception; the printed answer key nevertheless identifies statement 3 as the intended answer. Other-exam relevance: simple random sampling, finite-population correction and variance comparison are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is topic overlap, not a claim that this exact question appeared in those other examinations.

items.topic: sampling-t5 · circular systematic sampling; unbiasedness of the sample mean and bias of the usual sample variance
items.stem: For circular systematic sampling, which of the following statements are correct?
statements: The sample mean is an unbiased estimator of the population mean, but the usual sample variance is not an unbiased estimator of the population variance.
The sample mean and the usual sample variance are unbiased estimators of the population mean and population variance, respectively.
The sample mean is not an unbiased estimator of the population mean, but the usual sample variance is an unbiased estimator of the population variance.
Neither the sample mean nor the usual sample variance is an unbiased estimator of its population counterpart.

A.why: Circular systematic sampling gives every population unit the same first-order inclusion probability, so the design expectation of the sample mean is the population mean. The usual within-sample variance does not, in general, estimate the population variance without bias.

B.why: The sample mean is unbiased, but the usual sample variance is not generally unbiased under this design.

C.why: The sample mean is design-unbiased because each unit has the same chance of appearing in the sample.

D.why: The sample mean is unbiased, so it is incorrect to say that neither estimator is unbiased.

items.explanation: The answer key on page 63 of the supplied Estimation CSIR NET PDF gives Question 37 as statement 1. We can understand the two parts separately. First, circular systematic sampling chooses a random start and then selects units at a fixed interval around the ordered population. Every population unit has the same first-order inclusion probability. Therefore, when we average the sample mean over all possible random starts, each population value receives the same weight, and the expected sample mean equals the population mean. So the sample mean is unbiased. Second, the usual sample variance is calculated only from the units that appear together in the realised systematic sample. Systematic samples do not contain all possible combinations of units; many pairs have zero probability of appearing together. As a result, the usual sample variance does not, in general, average to the population variance over the design. Thus statement 1 alone is correct, option A. Remember: an estimator can be unbiased for the mean even when the familiar sample-variance formula is not an unbiased estimator of population variance under that sampling design. Other-exam relevance: systematic sampling, inclusion probabilities and design-based unbiasedness are relevant to UGC NET/JRF Statistics, GATE Statistics and State SET Statistics syllabi. This is syllabus overlap, not a claim that this exact CSIR question appeared in those examinations.
